column6: The commentary cites God hurling truth against falsehood; Daniel's hostile horn casts truth to the ground while acting successfully, reversing the agent, direction and immediate outcome of the cast.
The commentary's penetrating projectile carries haqq; Jeremiah calls the deceitful tongue a deadly arrow even as the speaker offers a neighbor peace, assigning the weapon to false speech.
The commentary's truth is launched at falsehood; the plotters sharpen their tongues like swords and aim bitter words like arrows, making malicious speech the projectile instead.
The commentary's unswerving strike serves haqq; the conspirators shoot suddenly at the blameless without fear, giving the preceding verbal arrows an innocent human target.
The commentary presents a directed blow against falsehood; after addressing a deceitful tongue, the psalm answers it with a warrior's sharp arrows and burning coals.
The commentary says truth thrown upon falsehood breaks its target; God compares his word to fire and to a hammer that breaks rock, making authoritative speech a destroying force.
The commentary's truth becomes an effective weapon; God tells Jeremiah he will make the words in the prophet's mouth fire and this people wood for it to consume.
The commentary's haqq is a blow that reaches its object; God says he has hewn the people by prophets and killed them with the words of his mouth, linking speech to a bodily strike.

The commentary's worked blow does not swerve or miss; God's outgoing word will not return empty but will accomplish the purpose for which he sent it, making successful arrival central without a weapon image.
The commentary's projectile carries truth toward falsehood; Proverbs pictures a reckless person throwing firebrands, arrows and death before identifying deceptive treatment of a neighbor.
The commentary's directed action is answerable to haqq; the comparison's target is a person who deceives a neighbor and says he was only joking, exposing a false excuse for the preceding projectiles.

column5: word lodged like arrow in flesh
column6: The commentary brings together a penetrating weapon, an inward bodily destination and speech; Sirach likens a word lodged inside a fool to an arrow stuck in a person's thigh, though its point is the fool's urge to let the word out.
The commentary hears an inward striking force in haqq; Sirach says a tongue's blow can break bones, treating speech as bodily violence in a warning about harmful talk.
The commentary's verbal truth has a weapon's effect; Sirach compares deaths by sword with still more falls caused by the tongue, emphasizing the dangerous reach of words.

column5: worker handles word of truth rightly
column6: The commentary joins amal as directed effort to haqq as an unswerving result; Timothy is told to be an approved worker who handles the word of truth rightly and need not be ashamed.

column5: word of truth and righteous weapons
column6: The commentary lets truth function as a directed weapon; Paul places the word of truth and God's power beside weapons of righteousness in his account of ministry.
The commentary's truth strikes what has deviated; the speaker commands repentance and threatens to fight the offenders with the sword of his mouth, giving verbal judgment a stated target.
The commentary reads haqq as a penetrating projectile; John's vision gives the exalted figure a sharp two edged sword issuing from his mouth, a recurring image of forceful utterance.
The commentary's blow reaches the inside; the continuation of the piercing word says no creature is hidden and all are exposed before God, identifying what the inward reach discloses.
The commentary's directed work and haqq meet in combat imagery; the exhortation has believers fasten truth around the waist as part of their equipment before naming the word as a sword.
The exception names righteous action and sabr in response to loss; Paul describes people seeking eternal life through patient persistence in good work.
The commentary treats right action as force aimed on a line; Timothy is told to pursue righteousness, faith and endurance, putting the verse's qualities into directed motion.
The exception combines deeds and patience; the address to Ephesus names its works, toil and endurance and says it cannot bear evil people.
The commentary's right effort must keep its course; the same address says the community has endured for the speaker's name and has not grown weary.
The exception joins faith with sabr; this call amid captivity and death names the endurance and faith of the saints, an earlier formulation of the combination.
The commentary pairs truth counsel with patience; the address says its hearers have kept the speaker's word of endurance, joining faithful response to utterance with perseverance.
The verse says believers mutually commend truth; Colossians asks that Christ's word dwell in them as they teach and admonish one another in wisdom, supplying an explicit communal verbal act.
The verse's tawasaw bil haqq is mutual; Ephesians tells each person to put off falsehood and speak truth with a neighbor because they belong to one another.
The verse joins reciprocal counsel and sabr; Paul asks the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient with everyone.
The verse couples recommending truth with patience; Timothy is instructed to proclaim the word, correct and exhort with complete patience and teaching.

column5: word held through labor without vain result
column6: The commentary contrasts lost effort with a true directed word; Paul asks the community to hold fast the word of life so he can say he neither ran nor labored in vain.
The commentary's weapon image meets its mutual exhortation; Proverbs says iron sharpens iron as one person sharpens another, giving reciprocal correction the action of preparing a blade.
The commentary combines an operated weapon with mutual guidance toward truth; Proverbs says battle is waged by wise guidance and victory comes through many counselors.
The commentary's exhortation prevents departure from the true line; Proverbs puts heeding instruction on a path to life and says rejecting reproof leads astray.

column5: foolish way versus listening to counsel
column6: The commentary's loss is a missed course that mutual truth can correct; Proverbs contrasts a fool whose way is right in his own eyes with a wise person who listens to advice.

column5: false way rejected by right precepts
column6: The commentary places haqq opposite deviation; the psalmist regards all God's precepts as right and hates every false way, stating both sides of that choice together.

column5: false way put away by teaching
column6: The commentary's counsel of truth wards off a wrong line; the psalmist asks for the false way to be removed and for God's law to be graciously taught.
The commentary's good action follows an unswerving course; the psalmist holds his feet back from every evil way in order to keep God's word.
The commentary cites God sending truth as a force; the psalmist asks God to send light and truth to lead him to the holy hill, turning the sent truth into guidance along a route.
The commentary makes haqq the line that prevents loss; the psalmist asks God to guide him in truth and teach him, joining truthful instruction to a directed path.
The commentary contrasts the accurate course with loss by deviation; Proverbs says integrity guides the upright while the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them.

column5: evil devisers stray, good devisers gain fidelity
column6: The commentary opposes wrong direction to effective good action; Proverbs asks whether devisers of evil go astray and promises steadfast love and faithfulness to devisers of good.
The commentary makes loss a wrong course; the psalm contrasts the Lord's knowledge of the righteous way with the way of the wicked that perishes, giving each path its outcome.

column5: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's haqq directs action without deviation; Wisdom says rulers decree justice by her, using Hebrew ḥqq for an authoritative prescription joined to right judgment.

column5: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's haqq is the true course; Isaiah condemns rulers who enact unjust decrees, showing that a Hebrew ḥqq prescription can itself be crooked rather than true.

column5: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary gives human work an intended outcome yet places humanity in loss; the psalm says builders labor in vain unless the Lord builds the house, making Hebrew toil's success conditional.

column5: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary couples effective work to mutual counsel; Qoheleth says two are better than one because they have a good reward for their Hebrew toil, supplying a concrete benefit to shared effort.

column5: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary calls loss a moral deviation; Qoheleth describes a wealthy person lacking nothing desired yet unable to enjoy it, showing that absence of Hebrew material lack can still coexist with frustrated gain.

column5: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's loss follows a wrong course; a covenant curse says Israel will serve enemies in hunger, thirst and lack of everything, making Hebrew deficiency an outcome of disobedience in its context.

column5: unjust decree turns needy from justice
column6: The commentary's haqq is a blow that does not deviate; the continuation of Isaiah's unjust decrees says they turn the needy aside from justice, spelling out the harmful deviation enacted by such rules.

The commentary gives truth an effective strike against falsehood; Isaiah instead portrays truth stumbling in the public square while justice is turned back, a specific reversal of truth's immediate success.

column5: truth absent and upright person prey
column6: The commentary says the faithful escape loss by truth and right conduct; Isaiah says truth is missing and the one who turns from evil becomes prey, exposing a contrary outcome for the upright.
The commentary's haqq functions through a forceful utterance; Jesus asks that his disciples be sanctified in truth and identifies God's word as truth, giving the verbal and moral terms a direct link.
The commentary opposes truth to falsehood as a forceful conflict; Jesus calls the devil a murderer and the father of lies, giving false speech a destructive agent rather than a neutral wrong turn.

The commentary's effective truth is cast against its opponent; James calls the tongue a fire that stains the body and sets a life's course ablaze, a contrary example of speech as uncontrolled destructive force.
The verse's exception combines righteous deeds and patience; Peter asks those who suffer in accordance with God's will to entrust themselves to the faithful Creator while continuing to do good.
